doc.title: Kenny Barron — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: How the Sphere quartet with Charlie Rouse formed
summary: The Carter-quartet trio of Barron, Buster Williams and Ben Riley adds Charlie Rouse and plans a Monk album.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis

blocks.x: Since we brought up Sphere, in the chronology that we’ve been following as far as your career development, we just took these few little tangents, but I felt it was necessary to really talk about the education, because that seems to be inextricable from the music now.
Whereas it wasn’t that way when you were coming in.
So, Sphere. This – the pictures – I know this is not Kenny Barron. I know this is not Ben Riley. But you knew that, right? The way they mislabeled you guys?
Oh yeah. Wow. I forgot about that. I think people who knew us, they knew.

But, for me, this was important, because I was already into the music in 1982, and when Monk died, it was a blow to everybody for years, psychic and spiritually. You guys, you recorded this the day he died.

This was – as you say in the liner notes – these are great liner notes. Everyone gets a chance to participate in this. But this was something many years in the making, or at least conceptually – months. Let’s just say months, because you guys already had the trio. You, Buster, and . . .

. . . and Ben had already had the trio. For me, this was important. This was one of – this album and – this was key in my development. So if you could let the public know about the development of Sphere and give us that story.

It started out – as you mentioned, we had the trio, Ben Riley, Buster Williams, and myself. We had been part of the Ron Carter quartet, that rhythm section. When Ron broke the band up, we continued to work as a trio and also as a rhythm section for other guys who were coming to town, Eddie Harris or Lockjaw [Eddie Davis] and Sweets [Harry Edison]. We would be their rhythm section. So we said, maybe we should just get a horn player and have a quartet. It was Ben who came up with the idea of Charlie Rouse. He said, “Yeah, I just heard Rouse not too long ago. He really sounded great.” We got a gig at – it was a place called Paulson’s. We got a gig and called Rouse. He made the gig, and it was a perfect fit. It just worked. Then, for the first record, we decided since we got two people in the band who had played with Monk, let’s do an album of Monk compositions. One of the things we decided we wanted to do was make sure the money went into Monk’s publishing company. So we met with Don Sickler, who was handling Monk’s publishing company, found out which tunes were in his company. We should stop the tape.
